world.bio: Kitchen-garden coordinator at a Brunswick primary school (about 320 kids), running a program that has every class doing a garden session and a cooking session each week. Half my job is gardening with eight-year-olds, the other half is begging local businesses and parents for donations. Two days a week I work from the school's tiny garden shed office. I'm doing a part-time permaculture course on Thursday nights, I'm training a rescue greyhound named Biscuit, and my fifteen-year-old wants to leave school for a trade.
skills_assets: Kitchen-garden program for 320 students, with 12 teachers as regular partners
A garden of about 400 square metres with a chook run, a compost bay and an orchard of six fruit trees
The school's council-registered commercial kitchen (used mostly for the cooking classes)
A parent volunteer roster of about 25 people, of whom 8 are reliable
A network of local businesses: the Brunswick Bunnings, a nursery in Coburg, two cafes that give us coffee grounds

projects.name: Spring planting with the kids
projects.text: Spring planting with the kids starts in October: tomatoes, beans, zucchini, sunflowers. Problem: the raised beds are rotting. Twelve beds built eight years ago from untreated pine, and half have collapsed or are held together with cable ties. The grant I'd applied for from a local foundation to replace them with hardwood fell through in August. We have six usable beds for 320 kids.

projects.name: Weekend use of the school kitchen
projects.text: The school kitchen is council-registered for commercial use. On weekends it sits empty, spotless, and I keep thinking it should be used. I raised it with the principal at a staff meeting and she said she's open to community use as long as there's an agreement and insurance. I haven't had time to follow it up.

projects.name: Permaculture course
projects.text: Thursday nights at a community centre in Northcote. We are on soil biology. Last week the teacher asked what our worst pest was; I said 'the Year 4 boys with watering cans'.

notes.text: Principal called me in. The foundation said no on the garden beds. They said the program is great but the funding round was oversubscribed. I smiled and said thank you and then went to the shed and ate a whole packet of Tim Tams.

Spent the morning crawling around the beds with a screwdriver, testing the timber. Four beds will not survive a spring. Two are held together by luck. The kids were so excited about planting. I said we might have to do containers. A girl in Grade 3 asked, 'Can we do tomatoes in buckets?' I said yes. She said 'my nonna does that'.
Biscuit the greyhound chewed a hole in my sneaker. We're working on 'leave it'. He's learning faster than my teenager.

Rang around for timber donations. Bunnings has a community fund but the application takes six weeks. A local builder offered some offcuts but they're treated pine and I can't use treated pine near edible plants. A man at a sawmill in Thomastown said he might have spare hardwood sleepers. I left a message.
Parent meeting. Only eleven showed. I asked for volunteers for a build weekend. Three said maybe. One dad said, 'I'm not a carpenter, mate.' I said you don't have to be. I had to say it six times.

Argument with my son Liam about school. He wants to leave at the end of Year 10 and become an electrician's apprentice. I said finish Year 12. He said 'You wouldn't have finished if you didn't like the garden'. Which is frustrating and unfair and also kind of true.

Looked at the school kitchen at 6pm, after everyone had gone. Stainless steel benches, a big oven, six burners, all sitting there. A woman from the neighbourhood had once asked if she could use it for catering and I'd said no because I didn't know how. I should have asked.
Permaculture class: we did a site analysis of a hypothetical garden. I did mine on the school. The teacher said 'your biggest limiting factor is not soil, it's people'. I wrote that in my notebook.
Greyhound walk at the Merri Creek. Biscuit pulled toward a rabbit. I let go of the lead for half a second. He was back before I swore.

messages.text:
Helen: I'm sorry about the grant. Let's think about alternatives.
Kirsty: Containers, buckets, anything.
Helen: I'll talk to the P&C about funding.
Kirsty: Thanks.

Liam: Mum I got a bit of work experience with a sparky next week.
Kirsty: Oh? That's great.
Liam: You're not mad?
Kirsty: I'm just worried. Have fun.

Gus: I've got some hardwood sleepers, about 20, not pretty.
Kirsty: How much?
Gus: Give me a hundred bucks and some veggies in summer.
Kirsty: Deal. How do I get them?
Gus: You'd need a ute.

Mei: I can come help with building on a Saturday.
Kirsty: Brilliant.
Mei: My husband's a bit handy.
Kirsty: Bring him.
